The Great Train Robbery of 1900: A Forgotten Heist

Among the most infamous crimes in history, the Great Train Robbery of 1900 stands out for its sheer audacity, cunning, and brazen release of chaos on the unsuspecting British public. While many can recall the daring heist of the Flying Scotsman in 1963, when 15 masked thieves stole £2.6 million, most have never heard of the daring gang that robbed the Royal Mail train at lowering Haresley Moor near Tonypandy in Wales, getting away with a sum believed to be around £12 million in today's currency.

Exactly at 6 pm on June 7, 1900, a Northern Counties Committee goods train left Liverpool Street station with a guard, but no passenger service was created. It was, in fact, a "banksman" - a railway employee with a handcart of 10,000. four-pound notes and ï¿½100 notes to be relocated to the vaults in London. It consisted of 29 containers, known as weekday packets, bound for the Royal Mint in Brindley Street. Onboard was £92,009 – dwarfed by the haul of the 1963 heist.

The gang struck at Loughaber coal colliery station 35 miles northeast from Cardiff, pouncing with energy determination before the crew could notice them. The goods cars were part-flattened, allowing bandits to sort, remove, and, after escape, vanish into the Cornshân vales highways.
